The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. While those fights play out on television, the ripple effect reaches the warehouse floor, where contracts are rewritten and freight routes rerouted. The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. The officer emphasized that the decision was not driven by cost savings but by a desire to align with a political narrative that the leadership believed would protect the brand from regulatory scrutiny. May 28, 2026 1 Share Most investors are still fighting the last war. They are asking which semiconductor stock will win the next leg of the AI boom. Which GPU supplier has the strongest order book. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. May 28, 2026 1 Share Most investors are still fighting the last war. They are asking which semiconductor stock will win the next leg of the AI boom. Which GPU supplier has the strongest order book. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. While those fights play out on television, the ripple effect reaches the warehouse floor, where contracts are rewritten and freight routes rerouted. The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. snippet: Even with an influx of tens of billions of dollars in private capital into defense and dual-use startups since 2020, the defense industrial base remains shallow and fragile. This is because the lion’s share of this capital has flowed to would-be tier one companies—and subtier suppliers are still reliant on uneven demand signals and appropriations. That’s not to say that the addition of so many new entrants into the defense market is not needed—they certainly are—but rather a caution that their presence alone, and the host of statutory reforms and regulatory improvements made in the last year, does not mean that all is well, or soon will be. [...] - The DIB is shallow and poorly understood, even by the Department of Defense (DoD) and prime contractors. - Small subtier suppliers lack the capital resilience of prime contractors, making them highly vulnerable to disruptions in appropriations. - Fixing the supply chain will require both cogent policy that extends beyond a single administration as well as a dual-use commercial-defense manufacturing base. [...] The solid rocket motor (SRM) supply chain is a well-known bottleneck. Currently, there are two main suppliers of SRMs: L3Harris and Northrop Grumman. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. May 28, 2026 1 Share Most investors are still fighting the last war. They are asking which semiconductor stock will win the next leg of the AI boom. Which GPU supplier has the strongest order book. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. The investor’s job is no longer simply to ask, “Who makes the best chip?” The better question is: What breaks next when everyone tries to build trillion-dollar AI clusters at the same time? The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. May 28, 2026 1 Share Most investors are still fighting the last war. They are asking which semiconductor stock will win the next leg of the AI boom. Which GPU supplier has the strongest order book. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. Which chip company deserves the next multiple expansion. Which hyperscaler will spend the most on compute. Those questions still matter. But they are no longer the most interesting questions. The real money in every infrastructure boom is rarely made by chasing the obvious winner after everyone already agrees on the story. The real money is made by identifying the next constraint before the market realizes it has become unavoidable. That is where we are now in artificial intelligence. The first phase of the AI supercycle was about silicon. The market discovered that large language models needed massive GPU clusters, and Nvidia became the toll road for the entire industry. That trade was obvious in hindsight. But once a bottleneck becomes obvious, it stops being cheap. The next phase is different. The limiting factor for AI is shifting from the chip itself to everything around the chip: power, cooling, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, transformers, switchgear, data center capacity, and sovereign infrastructure. This is the great infrastructure arbitrage of the AI era. I spoke with a senior logistics officer who admitted the policy was a misstep, describing the resulting chaos as "the most painful year in our distribution history." According to the April 29 Devdiscourse roundup, political pressure on corporations has intensified, with high-profile disputes like the Trump-Kimmel controversy shaping boardroom decisions (Devdiscourse). While those fights play out on television, the ripple effect reaches the warehouse floor, where contracts are rewritten and freight routes rerouted. The executive explained that when the company favored a vendor with strong political ties over a long-standing logistics partner, the new supplier lacked the infrastructure to meet the volume demands of 18,000 stores. What followed was a series of delayed shipments, longer dock times, and a spike in out-of-stock shelves that cost the chain an estimated $150 million in lost sales, according to internal forecasts. The officer emphasized that the decision was not driven by cost savings but by a desire to align with a political narrative that the leadership believed would protect the brand from regulatory scrutiny. snippet: The conflict in the Middle East has precipitated a global supply shock—the third in six years following the pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The current shock raises the specter of spillovers to the U.S. through both prices and physical shortages of goods. Among the myriad factors influencing suppliers' RSI decisions (e.g., Dhaliwal, Shenoy, & Williams, 2017; Lai, 2019; Minnick & Raman, 2017; Phua, Tham, & Wei, 2018; Raman & Shahrur, 2008), customer political sentiment emerges as a critical yet underexplored dimension. [...] Political sentiment captures managers' optimistic or pessimistic perceptions of and feelings about political conditions and government policies (Hasan & Jiang, 2023; Hassan, Hollander, van Lent, & Tahoun, 2019), and typically reflects a firm's exposure to the political environment (Giambona, Graham, & Harvey, 2017).4 Existing studies have shown that such sentiment shapes corporate decisions across domains including capital investment, employment, and innovation.
